Customize Cluster Storage
Copy page

Each cluster tier comes with a default set of resources. M10+ clusters provide the ability to customize your storage capacity.

Atlas provides the following storage configuration options, depending on the selected cloud provider and cluster tier.

Cluster Class

M40+ clusters offer multiple options, including:

Low CPU
General
Local NVMe SSD

All production environments can use the General option.

Select the Class box with your preferred speed. Changes to cluster class affect cost.

Low CPU Class

Generally, the Low CPU option offers a lower-cost alternative for applications that require more memory and fewer CPUs. This option includes half the vCPUs of an instance with the General option of the same tier. For example, a General M40 instance includes 4 vCPUs, while a Low CPU M40 instance includes 2 vCPUs. Depending on the cluster tier, this option may also include fewer max connections. To learn more, see Connection Limits and Cluster Tier.

NOTE

Atlas provisions storage for Low CPU and General clusters in gibibytes (GiB), despite the UI showing GB.

NVMe Storage

You can select the Local NVMe SSD storage option for some dedicated clusters that run on AWS or Azure. Locally attached ephemeral NVMe SSDs offer the highest level of speed and performance. Atlas provisions storage for NVMe clusters in gigabytes (GB).

A File Copy Based Initial Sync will always be used to sync all of the nodes of an NVME cluster whenever an initial sync is required.

NOTE

Atlas doesn't support NVMe clusters on Google Cloud.

Storage Capacity

To change the server data volume size, do one of the following tasks:

Move the slider until the text box displays your preferred disk size.

Specify the exact disk size in the text box.

For Azure-specific instructions, see Change Storage Capacity and IOPS on Azure.

Changes to storage capacity affect cost.

NOTE

MongoDB uses a small portion of your specified storage capacity for buffer files, journal files, and log files to ensure proper cluster operation. In no-overwrite storage engines like the WiredTiger storage engine, you should expect to use approximately 20% more disk space than your compressed data occupies.

Oplog Size Behavior

Atlas manages the cluster's oplog size and its entries differently, depending on whether storage auto-scaling is enabled for the cluster.

Atlas enables cluster storage auto-scaling by default. If you choose to use storage auto-scaling, Atlas manages the oplog entries based on the minimum oplog retention window (oplogMinRetentionHours) setting. The oplog entries are time-stamped. The oplog window is the time difference between the newest and the oldest timestamps in the oplog.

By default, Atlas sets the minimum oplog retention window to 24 hours. This means that, unless you set the minimum oplog retention window to a particular custom value, the mongod for the Atlas cluster retains all oplog entries for at least 24 hours and until the oplog reaches the maximum size that MongoDB best practices permit.

You can set the minimum oplog retention window to a particular value in the Atlas UI. For storage auto-scaling to complete successfully, Atlas requires the minimum oplog retention window (oplogMinRetentionHours) up to (60 seconds) * (GB of disk space configured).

If the cluster's storage capacity decreases, Atlas automatically scales the oplog size down to ensure it fits in the decreased storage size.

NOTE

In some high-volume bulk write scenarios, such as migrations, the cluster might not maintain the configured minimum oplog retention window. Plan migrations and other write-intensive operations accordingly.

You can opt out of cluster storage auto-scaling by un-checking the Storage Scaling checkbox in the Auto-scale section. If you opt out of storage auto-scaling, Atlas manages the oplog size as follows:

If you don't specify the oplog size in the UI, Atlas sets the oplog size to:

5% of the disk size when you create a cluster, for General and Low-CPU clusters

10% of the disk size for clusters with NVMe storage.

For dedicated clusters that use EBS (non-NVMe) storage, Atlas automatically scales the oplog size to match the new disk size when you change the storage size. For clusters with NVMe storage, oplog size is tied to the instance size rather than the disk size, since NVMe storage can't be resized independently. Atlas automatically syncs the oplog size with the new instance size when you change your cluster's tier.

You may choose to scale up the oplog size when you scale up the cluster's storage. In this case, manually set the oplog size to a particular value when you create a cluster. Atlas automatically scales the oplog size when you increase the cluster's storage, as follows:

For General and Low-CPU clusters, the oplog size scales up to remain at 5% of the storage capacity, not to exceed a certain maximum determined according to MongoDB best practices.

For clusters with NVMe storage, the oplog size scales up to remain at 10% of the storage capacity, not to exceed a certain maximum determined according to MongoDB best practices.

If you scale down the cluster's storage, Atlas uses the previous oplog-to-disk ratio to scale down the oplog proportionately. For example, if you scale from 100 GB to 50 GB with an oplog of 25 GB (ratio of 0.25), the new oplog size would also have a ratio of 0.25, which would make it 12.5 GB. The only exception is if the new oplog size is less than 5% of the storage capacity (or less than 10% for NVMe storage). In that case, Atlas uses the higher value for the oplog size, which would be 5% of the storage capacity (10% for NVMe storage).

Change Storage Capacity or IOPS on AWS

Atlas handles changes differently based on whether you want to increase or decrease storage capacity or storage throughput (IOPS) on AWS.

IMPORTANT

You can make a maximum of 4 EBS volume modifications within any 24-hour period. If you reach this limit, Atlas cannot modify your cluster's disk until the 24-hour window resets.

Increase Capacity or Throughput

If previous changes are completed, AWS usually takes about six hours to increase storage capacity or IOPS. However, this time frame can vary depending on the data size stored on disk. To learn more, see the AWS documentation. Atlas supports more changes within the time frame for volume modification changes.

AWS supports extended storage for clusters which meet the following criteria:

The cluster is either General or Low-CPU class

The cluster is single-region.

Extended storage is available for M40 tier and higher clusters with the following limitations:

M40: up to 4TB

M50/M60: up to 8TB

M80+: up to 14TB

To change your cluster's tier, see Modify a Cluster.

If you enable extended storage, this slows down initial syncs and cross-project snapshot restores, and can reduce high availability. Enabling extended storage is a temporary solution for clusters that might require additional storage capacity in the future. We recommend that you enable sharding for long-term expanded storage capacity.

How Atlas handles additional changes within a given period depends on AWS limits for EBS volume modifications. AWS restricts EBS volume size and throughput adjustments to a maximum of four modifications per volume within a rolling 24-hour period. After this limit is reached, Atlas delays additional storage capacity or IOPS changes for that volume until AWS allows another modification.

For the first change, Atlas modifies data volumes in place without downtime when increasing disk size.

For subsequent disk size increases:

Data Volume Size
	
Time Since Last Storage Change
	
Action Atlas Takes



Less than 1TB

	

Less than 6 hours

	

Atlas provisions new volumes and syncs the data from the old volumes. If Atlas provisions new volumes, you can access your cluster. You can't access nodes that AWS modifies until AWS attaches the new volume.




Less than 1TB

	

6 hours or more

	

Atlas waits until the cooldown period expires, then modifies the hosts' data volumes in place without downtime.




More than 1TB

	

Less than volume modification cooldown period (6 hours per TB)

	

Atlas provisions new volumes and syncs the data from the old volumes. If Atlas provisions new volumes, you can access your cluster. You can't access nodes that AWS modifies until AWS attaches the new volume.




More than 1TB

	

Volume modification cooldown period or more (6 hours per TB)

	

Atlas waits until the cooldown period expires, then modifies the hosts' data volumes in place without downtime. This takes less time than provisioning new volumes and syncing data from the old to the new volumes. If you modify the disk size within 4 hours of a previous disk modification, Atlas prioritizes compute upscaling first, then disk modification.

Before you apply your storage capacity or IOPS increases, the Review Changes page describes how Atlas approaches the increase.

The Clusters page displays a banner if Atlas is waiting for AWS to allow another volume modification before changing your cluster's storage capacity or IOPS:

Some EBS volume changes are delayed because AWS has reached the maximum number of allowed EBS volume modifications for this volume within a 24-hour period.

These behaviors apply when Atlas changes capacity during auto-scaling.

To learn more about AWS's limitations, see the AWS documentation.

Decrease Capacity or Throughput

AWS doesn't allow you to reduce storage capacity in place.

Atlas can reduce storage capacity by first provisioning new volumes and then syncing data from the old to the new volumes with an in-place data sync process. This works around the AWS limitation, but there is downtime on each node during the sync. Unlike capacity increases, Atlas always uses this process for capacity decreases, regardless of the volume modification cooldown period.

AWS does allow you to reduce IOPS without migrating data.

If the volume modification cooldown period has passed, Atlas reduces IOPS in place without restarting nodes. If the cooldown period has not passed, Atlas may provision new volumes and sync data, which causes a rolling restart.

Change Storage Capacity and IOPS on Azure

For Low CPU or General clusters deployed on Azure, you can extend IOPS and the data volumes' storage capacity in the Atlas UI.

If you increase disk storage for Low CPU or General clusters, you can:

Receive more IOPS on clusters in the same cluster tier.

Use these clusters for hosting applications with high IO workload requirements without having to configure sharding to spread the applications' workload across servers.

NOTE

Not all Azure regions support extended storage. For details, see supported regions.

Azure has volume modification cooldown periods that might limit how frequently you can make storage changes.

IMPORTANT

For Azure clusters that support Extended Storage/IOPS, you can make up to four disk IOPS/throughput changes within any 24-hour period. If you reach this limit, Atlas replaces the virtual machine (VM) to bypass this limitation.

The following statements describe the options you have in the Atlas UI for IOPS and storage management on Azure clusters.

Initially, when you choose an Azure Low CPU or General cluster, Atlas assigns the default storage size and IOPS based on the tier you choose.

Depending on the specific characteristics of the storage volumes used in your region and whether the cluster is in the region that supports extended storage, you can do one of the following actions:

If your region doesn't support extended storage, you can change storage capacity only in preset amounts and can't change the IOPS using the slider.

If your region supports extended storage, you can use the Storage slider to increase the default storage capacity within the same tier. Atlas also increases IOPS to correspond to the increased storage size.

If, after you increase the storage volume's size, the increased number of IOPS still isn't sufficient, and the cluster's tier is in a region that supports extended storage, you can further extend the number of IOPS using the IOPS slider, without changing the cluster tier.

In addition, you can also expand the total cluster storage beyond the default limits for the cluster's tier in regions that support extended storage. You enable extended storage sizes in the Project Settings.

NOTE

When increasing IOPS for a cluster deployed on Azure, values are limited to the cluster tier's maximum IOPS.

The following sections describe how to increase the storage size and IOPS.

Change Data Volume Size on Azure

Configure Extended Storage/IOPS on Azure

Change Data Volume Size on Azure

To change the server's data volume size:

View the cluster details.

In the Cluster tier > Storage section, you can do one of the following actions, depending on the region:

If your region supports extended storage, move the slider to the right and choose your preferred disk size.

The text box to the right of the slider changes dynamically and indicates the new disk size. Atlas also increases IOPS to correspond to the increased storage size.

If your region doesn't support extended storage, you can increase the disk capacity in preset amounts. In this case, Atlas doesn't increase IOPS.

For storage capacity increases, Atlas increases the storage capacity in place without copying data or performing an initial sync.

NOTE

If you change to another region or to a multi-region cluster, the specific storage volume capabilities or extended storage might be unavailable. The Atlas UI notifies you that your IOPS will be reduced. This change might impact the application's performance, the speed of restoring data from a backup, or copying backups from these regions to other regions. To preserve the same performance, continue using the same region. To learn more, see regions that support extended storage.

Azure doesn't allow decreasing the storage capacity in place. Atlas can reduce storage capacity by first provisioning new volumes and then syncing data from the old to the new volumes with an in-place data sync process. This works around the Azure limitation, but there is downtime on each node during the sync.

Before you apply your storage capacity reductions, the Review Changes page notifies you that Atlas triggers a rolling restart of your cluster when you make this change.

During this time, you can still access your cluster, but each node that Azure modifies remains unavailable until the node's data sync process completes. For large clusters, this process for each node might take several hours to complete.

To expand the total cluster storage beyond the limits for the cluster tier, you can enable extended storage in the Project Settings for regions that support extended storage.

Azure supports extended storage for clusters which meet the following criteria:

The cluster is either General or Low-CPU class

The cluster is single-region.

Extended storage is available for M40 tier and higher clusters with the following limitations:

M40: up to 4TB

M50/M60: up to 8TB

M80+: up to 14TB

To change your cluster's tier, see Modify a Cluster.

If you enable extended storage, this slows down initial syncs and cross-project snapshot restores, and can reduce high availability. Enabling extended storage is a temporary solution for clusters that might require additional storage capacity in the future. We recommend that you enable sharding for long-term expanded storage capacity.

Configure Extended Storage/IOPS on Azure

The following procedure describes how to obtain extended IOPS, on top of the number of IOPS that you receive when you increase the storage size within the same cluster tier.

You can change the number of IOPS for M40+ Atlas clusters for regions that support extended storage.

To extend the number of IOPS:

View the cluster details.

In the Cluster tier, change to the M40 or higher cluster tier. The IOPS slider displays in the IOPS section.

If you haven't already, increase the storage size.

If your application requires additional IOPS on top of increased IOPS that you received by increasing storage, you can extend IOPS further. Move the IOPS slider to the right and choose your preferred number of IOPS. Extending IOPS affects cost.

Change Storage Capacity on Google Cloud

Google Cloud supports extended storage for clusters which meet the following criteria:

The cluster is either General or Low-CPU class

The cluster is single-region.

Extended storage is available for M40 tier and higher clusters with the following limitations:

M40: up to 4TB

M50/M60: up to 8TB

M80+: up to 14TB

To change your cluster's tier, see Modify a Cluster.

If you enable extended storage, this slows down initial syncs and cross-project snapshot restores, and can reduce high availability. Enabling extended storage is a temporary solution for clusters that might require additional storage capacity in the future. We recommend that you enable sharding for long-term expanded storage capacity.

Unlike AWS, Google Cloud doesn't have volume modification cooldown periods. Therefore, storage changes can be made immediately without waiting for previous modifications to complete.

When you increase a cluster's storage capacity, Atlas modifies the size of the servers' data volumes in a rolling manner with zero downtime. Atlas increases the storage capacity in place without copying data or performing an initial sync.

However, Google Cloud doesn't allow in-place storage capacity reduction. If you reduce the storage capacity of a cluster, Atlas provisions new volumes, and then syncs data from the old to the new volumes with an in-place data sync process. This works around the Google Cloud limitation, but there is downtime on each node during the sync.

Before you apply your storage capacity reduction, the Review Changes page notifies you that Atlas triggers a rolling restart of your cluster when you make this change.

During this time, you can still access your cluster, but each node that Google Cloud modifies remains unavailable until the node's data sync process completes. For large clusters, this process for each node might take several hours to complete.

Atlas has disk capacity limits on single replica sets, scaling up to 4 TB for higher cluster tiers. To expand the total cluster storage beyond default limits, you can enable extended storage in the Project Settings. To accommodate further scaling in the future, enable sharding for long-term expansion.

Change Storage Capacity for Multi-Cloud Provider Clusters

Atlas selects the lowest common denominator across the three cloud providers. This ensures consistency across the multi-cloud deployment.

You can't adjust the IOPS for your multi-cloud cluster.

IOPS Types

M30+ clusters offer different options for customizing the amount of IOPS, depending on the cluster's cloud provider and cluster generation:

For clusters hosted on AWS you can use Provisioned IOPS and High Performance IOPS for Gen1 and Gen2 Dedicated clusters, respectively.

For clusters hosted on either AWS or Google Cloud, you can use Extended Standard IOPS for Gen2 Dedicated clusters.

NOTE

For Gen1 M40+ tier clusters, you can customize IOPS only for clusters in the General and Low CPU classes. You cannot customize IOPS for Gen1 clusters in the Local NVMe SSD class.

Provisioned IOPS and High Performance IOPS for AWS-hosted Clusters

Provisioned IOPS and High Performance IOPS let you customize the maximum IOPS rate for your AWS-hosted cluster with additional performance benefits. Provisioned IOPS and High Performance IOPS refer to the same concept, though Gen1 clusters use Provision IOPS in the Atlas UI and Gen2 clusters use High Performance IOPS. For simplicity, we use High Performance IOPS to refer to both here.

Standard IOPS use AWS General Purpose SSD volumes, which are designed to deliver their baseline performance 99% of the time. High Performance IOPS use AWS Provisioned IOPs SSD volumes, which are designed to deliver their provisioned performance 99.9% of the time.

Compared to standard IOPS, High Performance IOPS:

Deliver their configured IOPS rate more consistently.

Lower your cluster's p90 latency (measurement of the server's response time). 90 percent of server requests have responses faster than the p90 latency value, so a lower p90 latency value means a generally faster response time.

To learn more, see:

Amazon EBS volume types

Configure Provisioned IOPS and High Performance IOPS

Extended Standard IOPS

Gen2 Dedicated clusters on AWS or Google Cloud have a baseline minimum IOPS, on top of which you can provision additional IOPS:

For clusters with disk storage under 1000GB (1TB), this baseline is 3000 IOPS.

For clusters with disk storage over 1000GB, this baseline scales with storage at an IOPS-to-GB ratio of 3:1.

NOTE

Clusters hosted on AWS make a distinction between Standard IOPS and Provisioned or High Performance IOPS. This distinction stems from the cluster's underlying SSD volumes, and is exclusive to clusters hosted on AWS.

To learn more, see Provisioned IOPS and High Performance IOPS.

The following table shows non-exhaustive examples of how this baseline scales with various disk sizes:

Disk Storage
	
Baseline IOPS



500GB

	

3000




1000GB

	

3000




2000GB

4000GB

	

12000

To provision additional IOPS for your cluster, you can use Extended Standard IOPS for Gen2 clusters hosted on AWS or Google Cloud. Extended Standard IOPS allow you to provision up to:

80k IOPS for AWS Gen2 Dedicated clusters

160k IOPS for GCP Gen2 Dedicated clusters

As you increase IOPS, the cluster’s available disk throughput also increases.

For Gen2 Dedicated clusters, you provision additional IOPS and scale storage capacity independently, so scaling one doesn't necessitate scaling the other. Because provisioning additional IOPS and scaling storage capacity are independent, Atlas bills for each separately.

To learn more, see:

Gen2 Dedicated clusters

Configure IOPS for Gen2 Clusters

Configure the IOPS Rate
Standard IOPS for Gen1 Clusters

If you want your IOPS rate to scale automatically with your cluster's storage capacity, don't select Provision IOPS when you create your AWS Gen1 M30+ tier cluster. The cluster uses standard IOPS by default.

If you want to provision an exact standard IOPS value for your AWS cluster, see Provisioned and High Performance IOPS.

NOTE

Clusters hosted on AWS make a distinction between Standard IOPS and Provisioned or High Performance IOPS. This distinction stems from the cluster's underlying SSD volumes, and is exclusive to clusters hosted on AWS.

To learn more, see Provisioned IOPS and High Performance IOPS.

The minimum standard IOPS for M30+ tier clusters is 3000. The standard IOPS value remains at 3000 unless you set the cluster storage size to 1TB or more. If the storage for your M30+ cluster meets or exceeds 1TB, Atlas increases the standard IOPS rate using an IOPS to a storage ratio of 3:1, up to 16k IOPS for AWS network storage volumes.

Gen1 Local NVMe SSD class clusters must use standard IOPS.

Extended Standard IOPS for Gen2 Clusters

To provision additional IOPS for your cluster, you can use Extended Standard IOPS for Gen2 clusters hosted on AWS or Google Cloud. Extended Standard IOPS allow you to provision up to:

80k IOPS for AWS Gen2 Dedicated clusters

160k IOPS for GCP Gen2 Dedicated clusters

NOTE

Clusters hosted on AWS make a distinction between Standard IOPS and Provisioned or High Performance IOPS. This distinction stems from the cluster's underlying SSD volumes, and is exclusive to clusters hosted on AWS.

To learn more, see Provisioned IOPS and High Performance IOPS.

If your M30+ tier Gen2 Dedicated clusters is hosted on AWS, you must first select Standard next to IOPS under the Cluster Tier section.

Then, you can either:

Specify the exact IOPS rate in the text box, or

Move the slide bar below the IOPS options until the text box displays your preferred IOPS rate.

Provisioned and High Performance IOPS

High Performance IOPS are supported only for M30+ tier clusters on AWS. To use High Performance IOPS for your M30+ tier AWS cluster, next to IOPS under the Cluster Tier section, select one of the following options:

Provision IOPS if you are using Gen1 clusters.

High Performance IOPS if you are using Gen2 cluster.

Then, you can either:

Specify the exact IOPS rate in the text box, or

Move the slide bar below the IOPS options until the text box displays your preferred IOPS rate.

NOTE

The available provisioned IOPS range for a Gen1 cluster relates to disk storage capacity. Changing your Gen1 cluster's storage capacity changes the range of available provisioned IOPS.

The available High Performance IOPS range for a Gen2 cluster is unrelated to disk storage capacity.

Minimum Disk Capacity to RAM Ratios

Atlas enforces the following minimum ratios for given cluster tiers. This keeps cluster performance consistent with large datasets.

Instance sizes M10 to M40 have a ratio of disk capacity to system memory of 60:1. Instance sizes greater than M40 have a ratio of 120:1.

EXAMPLE

To support 3 TB (or 3,072 GB) of disk capacity, select a cluster tier with a minimum of 32 GB of RAM. This would be M50 or greater.

Atlas has disk capacity limits on single replica sets, scaling up to 4 TB for higher cluster tiers. To expand the total cluster storage beyond default limits, you can enable extended storage in the Project Settings. To accommodate further scaling in the future, enable sharding for long-term expansion.

TIP

To learn more about the default resources and available configuration options for each cloud service provider, see:

AWS Configuration Options

GCP Configuration Options

Azure Configuration Options.

Auto-Scale Cluster Tier and Storage Capacity

Atlas cluster tier reactive auto-scaling is available for all dedicated cluster tiers under the General and the Low-CPU cluster classes.

For new clusters, Atlas automatically enables cluster tier auto-scaling and storage auto-scaling.

Use Auto-scale options to configure your cluster to automatically scale your cluster tier, storage capacity, or both in response to cluster usage.

IMPORTANT

During a migration, if you restore a snapshot with a larger size than the storage capacity of the destination cluster, the cluster does not automatically scale.

You can opt out of cluster tier and storage auto-scaling. To learn more, see How Atlas Scales Cluster Tier and How Atlas Scales Cluster Storage.
